channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: MIA Watchlist: Track whether the US-Iran war widens and Brent holds above USD 90, the 22 July Section 301 duties on Brazil and the Russian-oil tariff bill, the late-July Fed and ECB meetings, and China stimulus after 4.3% growth.
item.description:
• Hormuz and oil: whether the seventh-night strikes and first US casualties tip into a wider regional war, and whether Brent holds above USD 90 as the IEA-flagged reserve buffer runs down.
  • Tariff fronts: the 22 July start of US Section 301 duties on Brazil, Brazil's response, and the Senate vote path for up to 100% tariffs on China, India and three others over Russian oil.
  • Central banks: the late-July Fed (28–29) and ECB meetings — a possible US move toward a September hike versus an ECB hold, both driven by war-energy inflation.
  • China stimulus and slowdown: whether the Central Committee launches additional stimulus after Q2 GDP of 4.3%, and how far the high-tech and robotics surge offsets property weakness.
  • Europe's chemical base: the ETS-softening negotiations (several months), further VCI capacity signals, and Japan's naphtha-driven shift to biomass plastics as a feedstock-security indicator.

item.title: India launched its first privately developed orbital rocket, is betting over USD 21bn on semiconductors to reach the global top five by 2032, and grew April–May exports 14.66% to USD 162.7bn — even as inflation topped the RBI's 4% target.
item.description:
India is building industrial resilience on several tracks at once. Skyroot's Vikram-1 became the country's first privately developed orbital rocket on 18 July, placing payloads into a 450-km orbit and signalling a maturing private space sector. On chips, New Delhi has committed over USD 21bn — including the INR 1.27tn Semicon 2.0 scheme — targeting four to six fabs, several compound-semiconductor plants and ten assembly-and-test facilities within five years, and a top-five global position by 2032, building on Semicon 1's INR 1.64 lakh crore and 12 projects underway. Trade momentum is strong: April–May exports rose 14.66% to USD 162.7bn, with shipments to ASEAN up 66.9% and to Africa up 53.1%, diversifying away from Western markets. The main soft spot is prices — RBI Governor Malhotra flagged that inflation has topped the 4% target for the first time in about eighteen months, driven by supply-side factors and Iran-war and monsoon risks, keeping the bank in "wait and watch" mode at a 5.25% rate.

Industry Impact

India is an increasingly important growth market and manufacturing base for ACS. Its semiconductor and space build-out expands demand for specialty adhesives, coatings and encapsulants, while rapid export growth and supply-chain diversification make it a more attractive production and export hub — especially as India's import-substitution drive (see other insight in prior alerts) explicitly targets chemicals. Weigh serving the market through local production versus exports, track the semiconductor-fab rollout for materials demand, and watch inflation and monsoon risk as near-term signals for construction- and consumption-linked ACS volumes.

Business Standard | The Hindu Business Line | Business Standard | The Economic Times | The Economic Times | The Economic Times

item.title: Japanese retailers and municipalities are switching to biomass plastics as the Iran war squeezes naphtha imports, while the IEA warns critical-mineral supply security is deteriorating on rising concentration and export restrictions.
item.description:
Two developments frame input security from different angles. In Japan, the Middle East war is straining naphtha supply — about 40% is imported from the region — prompting retailers and municipalities to switch to plant-based biomass plastics; bioplastic maker Rice Resin saw consultation requests rise three- to fivefold since the conflict began. It is an early, concrete sign of scarcity in petroleum-derived materials that feed paints, solvents and packaging. Separately, the IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 warns that supply security is worsening: concentration in a few countries, declining investment and rising export restrictions are undermining the resilience of chains critical to the energy transition, high-tech and defence, with prices climbing again through 2025 and early 2026. Read alongside the last alert's USD 6.5tn rare-earth risk warning, the message is consistent — the inputs underpinning industrial production are becoming less secure and more politicised.

Industry Impact

This is squarely ACS-relevant. Naphtha and solvents are foundational to coatings and adhesives, and a squeeze acute enough to drive Japanese substitution is a live availability warning for the sector — and a spur to accelerate bio-based and non-fossil raw-material sourcing. The critical-minerals deterioration bears indirectly on ACS through customer industries (electronics, batteries, defence, autos) whose demand for adhesives and coatings depends on secure mineral supply. Model naphtha and solvent security explicitly, evaluate bio-based feedstock options, and treat input availability — not just price — as a strategic planning variable.

JIJI Press | The Nation | Kompas.com | Nihon Keizai Shimbun

item.title: Defence will fill half of a record 1,600 exhibitors at the Farnborough Airshow (20–24 July) as arms makers struggle to meet weapons demand; Saab's Q2 profit jumped, Airbus won a USD 19bn A220 order, and analysts see primes keeping 80%+ of the market.
item.description:
The airshow captures a decisive tilt toward defence. With civil jet and engine output still recovering slowly amid supply-chain constraints, weapons have moved to the centre of the event, pushing the traditional Boeing–Airbus commercial contest down the agenda. The order book reflects a broader boom: Saab reported Q2 operating profit of SEK 2.79bn (up from SEK 1.98bn) on sales up 28.8%, backed by Gripen E orders for Ukraine and Brazil, an A26 submarine deal with Poland and NATO GlobalEye interest. Civil aerospace is not absent — Airbus won a USD 19bn order for 150 Canadian-built A220s from AirAsia, the largest ever for a Canadian-made commercial aircraft, and Rolls-Royce is seeking UK support to re-enter the narrowbody engine market on the back of a 40% profit jump. On market structure, BCG expects established primes to hold more than 80% of the weapons market through 2033 even as cheaper drone segments grow faster.

Industry Impact

Aerospace and defence are high-value ACS end-markets — structural adhesives, sealants and specialty coatings are integral to airframes, engines and defence platforms. A sustained defence build-out and recovering commercial-jet production together lift demand for qualified aerospace-grade materials, typically high-margin and specification-locked. The drone-market surge adds a faster-growing, if lower-value, materials segment. Prioritise qualification and capacity for aerospace and defence programmes, and track which platforms and primes win orders to align material supply with the durable demand from established contractors.

The Economic Times | Commercial Times | The Globe and Mail | The Times of India | The Guardian

item.title: Months of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries have caused a nationwide diesel crisis now squeezing farmers, while the EU sanctioned five ABS Electro firms over drone production and Putin thanked North Korea for its war support.
item.description:
The war's economic centre of gravity is shifting inside Russia. Sustained Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries have produced a nationwide fuel crisis — spiking diesel prices and long queues — that now compounds farmers' problems as fighting in the Sea of Azov chokes the Rostov region's main grain export outlet. Russia is hitting back at Ukraine's export capacity too, damaging a cargo ship and targeting fuel tanks and army-bound freight in strikes on Odesa-region ports. The EU tightened the screws, sanctioning executive Irina Kharisova and five ABS Electro companies for making drone components, with a 21st sanctions package targeting banks, crypto networks and oil traders under negotiation. The alliance backdrop is hardening: Putin publicly thanked North Korea — which has supplied troops and weapons — for its support, in exchange for financial, food, energy and military-technology help, signalling the conflict is entrenching rather than winding down.

Industry Impact

The direct ACS exposure is limited, but the second-order effects are real. Russia's refinery crisis tightens global refined-product and diesel markets that feed logistics costs across chemical supply chains, and disruption to Black Sea grain and fertiliser flows interacts with the Gulf fertiliser risk (see other insight in this alert) to keep agricultural-input markets volatile. A deeper, longer war sustains European defence demand — a positive for structural adhesives and coatings in defence programmes — while keeping energy-security risk elevated. Monitor diesel and refined-product prices as a logistics-cost input and track the 21st sanctions package for measures touching chemical or energy trade.

MarketScreener | Handelsblatt | Arab News | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Dawn

item.title: Trump told PM Carney he wants damages over wildfire smoke crossing into the northeast US and threatened higher Canadian tariffs, layering an environmental grievance onto a stalled USMCA renewal and a deepening Canadian manufacturing exodus.
item.description:
The new element is the fusion of a force-majeure event with trade policy. Hundreds of active Ontario wildfires pushed hazardous smoke across the border, triggering air-quality alerts from Minnesota to Maryland; Trump accused Canada of forest mismanagement, said the pollution's cost must be "added to the tariffs Canada is currently paying", and pressed Carney for damages. The threat lands on already strained ground. The US declined to extend the USMCA on 1 July over trade-deficit concerns, formal talks with Canada have yet to yield the concessions Washington wants, and Mexico has said it will not strike a separate deal that leaves Canada behind. The economic backdrop is a Canadian "manufacturing recession" now in its third year, with a KPMG survey finding more than four in ten Canadian firms have moved production to the US or are considering it. An environmental dispute is being turned into additional leverage in an unresolved trade renegotiation.

Industry Impact

Two channels matter for ACS. Physically, wildfire smoke and recurring air-quality emergencies disrupt construction and outdoor industrial activity — a demand base for coatings and sealants — and raise worker-safety and operating costs at exposed North American sites. Commercially, tariff escalation and USMCA uncertainty complicate cross-border chemical and materials flows, while the manufacturing shift toward the US redraws where ACS demand sits. Build climate resilience into North American logistics and site planning, and model tariff scenarios for US–Canada chemical trade as the USMCA impasse drags on.

The Economic Times | CBC | The Globe and Mail | The Globe and Mail

item.title: Moonshot AI's 2.8-trillion-parameter open-source Kimi K3 topped global coding benchmarks and triggered a US tech sell-off, while at WAIC Xi warned against AI monopoly and MIIT said China holds over half the world's humanoid-robot models.
item.description:
This is the clearest signal yet that China is closing the AI gap on Western terms. Kimi K3 — open-sourced and topping international coding charts — sent the S&P 500 and Nasdaq lower on fears US leadership is eroding; the Philadelphia Semiconductor index fell 1.8% toward its worst week since March, down over 20% from its late-June peak. US AI Czar David Sacks called the model "concerning" and argued heavy domestic regulation is crippling US innovation as rivals catch up. Beijing amplified the moment at the World AI Conference (17–20 July), where Xi urged open-source collaboration and warned against any single nation dominating AI — positioning China as the alternative to US dominance. The hardware story is just as striking: MIIT said China has developed 400-plus humanoid-robot models, over half the global total, and accounts for roughly 70% of global quadruped-robot sales, alongside domestic advances like a 14nm 3D AI chip unveiled at WAIC.

Industry Impact

The physical-AI and robotics build-out is a medium-term demand driver for ACS — robotics, electronics assembly and semiconductor packaging all use specialised adhesives, coatings and encapsulants — and China's lead concentrates that demand in its domestic supply chain. An open-source Chinese model ecosystem also accelerates AI adoption in manufacturing globally, including process optimisation relevant to chemical production. But rapid Chinese self-sufficiency in the underlying hardware and materials is a competitive threat. Track robotics- and semiconductor-linked material demand, and watch how quickly Chinese specialty-material suppliers scale alongside the robot build-out.

The Independent | The Times of India | The Times of India | Global Times | Xhby.net

item.title: China's growth slowed to 4.3% in Q2 (H1 4.7%), raising stimulus expectations, but the composition tells a different story: high-tech manufacturing value-added rose 13.3% and AI-linked output grew at double digits, the fastest at 57.3%.
item.description:
The headline weakness and the structural strength need to be read together. Q2 growth of 4.3% — the softest run in the year — put the full-year target in question, with Goldman Sachs warning it is at risk and experts expecting fresh stimulus at the next Central Committee meeting; property remains the drag. Yet beneath the slowdown, Beijing's advanced-manufacturing engine is accelerating. Above-scale industrial value-added rose 5.4% in H1, led by high-tech manufacturing up 13.3%, with "AI+"-driven output of integrated circuits, optical fibre, electronic components and industrial and service robots growing at double digits and the fastest segment up 57.3%. Equipment manufacturing rose 9.3% and now accounts for 37% of large-scale industry, while service retail sales grew 5.3%. The pattern is deliberate: China is answering weak domestic demand by doubling down on high-end manufacturing rather than broad consumer stimulus, even as it prepares targeted support.

Industry Impact

For ACS producers this is a two-sided signal. The high-tech and equipment surge sustains demand for specialty adhesives, coatings and encapsulants used in electronics, semiconductors and robotics, so China's industrial-materials demand keeps growing even as construction-linked demand softens. But the same drive accelerates Chinese self-sufficiency in advanced materials, a competitive threat over time. Position for AI- and equipment-manufacturing-linked material demand in China, watch the coming stimulus for construction and property signals, and track how fast Chinese suppliers close the specialty-chemical gap.

Chinatimes.com | Xhby.net | China Economic Net | Xhby.net

item.title: Bloomberg says the EU faces a "quandary" over a subsidised Chinese export wave hitting cars, machine tools and chemicals, as China's June car exports jumped over 70% to a record and German brands' China sales fell up to 32%.
item.description:
The strategic problem and its live evidence sit together. Bloomberg frames a new, bigger "China shock" — this time aimed at the advanced industries Europe views as core — where China's state-backed drive for self-sufficiency distorts trade and threatens to hollow out EU industry, leaving Brussels caught between inaction and retaliation-prone tariffs. The trade data show the pressure building: China exported 1.1 million cars in June, up over 70% and the first month ever above one million. The mirror image is German pain inside China, where a lowered luxury-tax threshold (to CNY 900,000) hit European makers hardest — H1 China sales fell 32% at Porsche, 28% at Mercedes, 20% at BMW and 19% at Audi, per the VDA. Beijing is simultaneously trying to cool destructive domestic price wars, with its industry ministry telling automakers to resist "irrational competition" and tighten safety and quality — a sign the export surge is partly overcapacity spilling outward.

Industry Impact

Automotive is a core ACS end-market, so this cuts both ways. Surging Chinese vehicle output sustains materials demand but shifts it toward Chinese-qualified suppliers, while shrinking German premium volumes in China erode a high-value demand pool for European ACS producers. The "chemicals" call-out in the export-onslaught narrative is a direct warning that Chinese competitive pressure is reaching the sector itself. Position to qualify into Chinese and Chinese-owned production lines, defend value in premium European automotive applications, and watch for EU trade-defence measures that could reshape chemical and automotive flows.

Bloomberg | Cinco Días | Handelsblatt | MarketScreener

item.title: At the 26th Franco-German Council in Brühl, Merz and Macron adopted two declarations on security and economic cooperation and framed the undervalued yuan and China's growing EU trade surplus as an "existential threat" to European manufacturing.
item.description:
The retreat consolidates the relationship after a bruising year and sharpens Europe's China stance. Building on the Nörvenich defence meeting, the two governments pledged to deepen security and industrial cooperation and to reach agreements across a broad agenda before year-end, explicitly timing the push ahead of France's 2027 election, where a Le Pen presidency could complicate joint work. The harder edge is on China: Macron and Merz jointly cast the "undervalued Chinese yuan" and Beijing's rising EU surplus as an existential risk to European industry — language Chinese state media rejected as oversimplified. Merz paired the tough framing with a diplomatic opening, saying he wants dialogue with China on exchange rates and overcapacity rather than a trade conflict, and calling Chinese stakes in Volkswagen plants a "last resort". The defence track remains unfinished — the collapsed FCAS fighter programme still overshadows cooperation — but the direction is a more assertive, coordinated Franco-German line on both defence-industrial capacity and China.

Industry Impact

The relevance is second-order but strategic. A coordinated Franco-German drive to protect European industry and rebuild defence-industrial capacity signals demand for advanced structural adhesives, coatings and sealants in aerospace, defence and rail, and shapes the trade-and-energy policy backdrop that determines whether European chemical and manufacturing production stays viable. The harder China line also raises the odds of new EU trade defence measures affecting chemical flows. Track the year-end deliverables and any move from rhetoric to concrete tariff or industrial-policy action on China.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | Global Times | Commercial Times

item.title: The European Commission softened the Emissions Trading System after pressure from the German chemical industry, Italy and Central Europe, delaying full decarbonisation toward 2048, as the VCI reported German chemical and pharma output down 3% in H1 2026.
item.description:
These two items describe cause and effect. The pain is quantified by the VCI: German chemical and pharmaceutical output fell 3% year-on-year in H1, sales slipped 1% to EUR 106bn, and investment dropped for a third consecutive year, prompting a cut in the full-year production forecast to -1.5% amid underused plants, weak exports, high costs and fierce international competition. Brussels' response is a direct concession to that distress. The Commission proposed slowing the ETS's annual cap reduction (from 4.4% toward 3.7% after 2030 and softer thereafter), extending free allowances for firms that commit to decarbonising, pushing the full phase-out of free quotas to 2038 from 2034, and effectively moving heavy-industry carbon neutrality toward 2048 from 2039 — while extending the ETS to aviation and waste. It is an explicit acknowledgement that the previous trajectory was, in Le Figaro's framing, "unrealistic" for European industry.

Industry Impact

This is the most directly ACS-relevant cluster in the alert. Chemicals are the feedstock base for adhesives, coatings and sealants, so both the health of Europe's chemical sector and its regulatory cost burden bear directly on local supply and competitiveness. The ETS softening lowers a major cost and compliance headwind for European producers and buys time, but the underlying VCI numbers show the sector is still contracting. Treat the carbon-market relief as a partial, contested reprieve rather than a turnaround, factor the revised phase-out timeline into European investment and site decisions, and keep monitoring capacity utilisation as the real health signal.

Die Zeit | Le Figaro | Yahoo! Finance France | El País

item.title: The US will impose 25% duties on Brazilian goods from 22 July — its first Section 301 action — while 60-plus senators reintroduced a bill threatening up to 100% tariffs on China, India and three others for buying Russian oil.
item.description:
Two distinct escalations share one logic: tariffs as a reusable geopolitical tool. The Brazil action is the debut of Trump's revised Section 301 strategy, covering electrical equipment, paper, apparel, sugar, footwear, machinery, ethanol and furniture, with beef, coffee, rare earths, energy and aircraft exempted; USTR Greer justified it by pointing to Brazilian tariff concessions to India and Mexico not extended to the US. Because it is a template, it matters well beyond Brazil. In parallel, the "Sanctioning Russia Act" was reintroduced with over 60 senators, refining an earlier blanket 500% tariff into targeted measures of up to 100% on the top five buyers of Russian oil and gas — China, India, Slovakia, Hungary and Azerbaijan — with an exemption for countries importing under 15% of Russian gas. India said it is monitoring closely and stressed its energy sourcing is strategy-driven; Washington's 25% India tariff last year, later reversed, suggests the threat is partly a negotiating lever.

Industry Impact

The direct ACS exposure to Brazil is modest, but the precedent is the point: a repeatable Section 301 engine raises the odds of sudden, country-specific duties on chemical inputs and finished goods anywhere. A 100% tariff on China and India — both major producers and consumers of chemical intermediates — would be a severe shock to global chemical trade even as a standing threat, and the "energy-share" exemption logic means exposure maps must now include the energy behind inputs, not just where they are made. Map tariff scenarios by country as well as product, and keep sourcing flexibility for lines that could be caught in a widening net.

Pakistan Today | LiveMint | The Times of India | The Economic Times | The Economic Times

item.title: The IMF cut 2026 global growth to 3% from 3.5%, blaming the Iran war, as US Fed officials signal a possible September hike on energy-driven inflation while the ECB holds — a widening policy split around the same shock.
item.description:
This confirms in the numbers what the last alert flagged as a risk. The IMF now sees global output slowing sharply to 3% in 2026, and pairs the downgrade with a longer-term message that AI, while a major force on productivity and labour markets, has so far delivered "automation without transformation" rather than quick gains. Central banks are pulling apart around the energy shock. In the US, persistent inflation and high energy costs have pushed Fed officials — Hammack, Logan and Vice Chair Jefferson — toward tightening, lifting the odds of a September hike to about 65% even as the July meeting is expected to hold at 3.50–3.75%. The ECB, by contrast, is likely to keep rates steady while holding a September hike in reserve, with oil and gas near its baseline scenario and euro-area inflation slowing more than expected. The common thread is that the war is now the dominant macro variable, and it is pushing policy toward tightening precisely as growth cools.

Industry Impact

For ACS producers this is the classic stagflation-lite squeeze: softer demand in construction and manufacturing end-markets alongside sticky input and energy costs. Diverging rates matter for financing and FX — a firmer US path raises dollar-funding costs and can move euro–dollar in ways that reshape export competitiveness. Build planning around weaker volumes and elevated costs together, favour pricing discipline and working-capital efficiency over volume-led assumptions, and watch the late-July Fed and ECB meetings as the near-term signposts for H2 demand and financing conditions.

The Express Tribune | Dünya Gazetesi | Financial Post | The Hindu Business Line

item.title: A seventh straight night of US strikes killed US soldiers for the first time in months and pushed Brent above USD 91, with the IEA warning the world's oil-price buffer is now too thin to absorb a full Hormuz closure.
item.description:
The delta since the last alert is a clear step up in intensity and cost. US strikes now systematically target Iran's logistics backbone — bridges, railways, the Bandar Abbas hinterland and a surveillance tower at Chabahar — while Iranian missiles killed US personnel at a Jordanian air base, the first American deaths in months, and the fighting spread to Syria, Kuwait and Qatar. Markets, calm through earlier rounds, finally broke: Brent rose above USD 90 on 19 July for the first time since mid-June, then 3.8% higher above USD 91 on 20 July, up roughly 12% on the week and dragging US pump prices toward USD 4/gallon. The forward risk has hardened. IEA chief Fatih Birol warns the inventory "shock absorber" that capped prices — a record 400-million-barrel coordinated release by 32 countries — is largely spent, so a genuine Hormuz closure would now transmit straight to price. Middle East producers are rushing to build cross-desert pipelines that bypass the strait, but analysts note pipelines remain vulnerable to the same low-cost attacks.

Industry Impact

For chemical and ACS producers the channel is feedstock and freight, and the buffer that protected margins is gone. Crude and naphtha set the cost floor for adhesives, coatings and sealants, and with reserves depleted the next disruption feeds through immediately. There is also a direct supply angle: the Gulf supplies about a third of world fertiliser exports and is integral to many base chemicals, so a prolonged blockade threatens availability, not just price. Plan H2 around elevated, spike-prone input costs, stress-test Gulf-routed cargoes for freight and insurance inflation, and treat a Hormuz break as a live scenario rather than a tail risk.

Handelsblatt | Axios | Financial Post | Cnyes.com | LiveMint | The Financial Times | Kompas.com

item.title: MIA Digest: The US-Iran war escalated with a seventh night of strikes, the first US deaths in months and Brent above USD 91; the IMF cut 2026 growth to 3%; and the US opened tariff fronts on Brazil and Russian-oil buyers.
item.description:
• Iran war: a seventh straight night of US strikes killed US soldiers for the first time in months and pushed Brent above USD 91, with the IEA warning the oil-price buffer is nearly spent.
  • Growth and rates: the IMF cut 2026 global growth to 3%, and central banks split — the Fed is edging toward a September hike while the ECB holds.
  • Tariff fronts: Washington will hit Brazil with 25% duties from 22 July (first Section 301 action) and a revised Senate bill threatens up to 100% on China, India and three others over Russian oil.
  • Europe bends on climate: Brussels softened the carbon market after chemical-sector pressure, even as German chemical output fell 3% and Merz and Macron called China an 'existential threat'.
  • China: Q2 GDP slowed to 4.3% but the high-tech engine roared — the Kimi K3 open-source model rattled US markets and Beijing now holds over half the world's humanoid-robot models.
